entry: Family of flowering plants in the order Solanales, known as the nightshades, containing approximately 2,700 species. Several are used as agricultural crops, medicinal plants and ornamental plants. Many members have high [[Alkaloid|alkaloid]] contents, making some highly toxic, but many, such as [[Tomato|tomatoes]], potatoes, eggplants and peppers, are commonly used in food around the world. Originating in [[South America]], the family now inhabits every continent except [[Antarctica]]. After the K–Pg extinction event it rapidly diversified, adapting to deserts, tundras, rainforests, plains and highlands and taking the form of trees, vines, shrubs and epiphytes. Nearly 80% of nightshades belong to the subfamily Solanoideae. The tobacco plant has long been used as a recreational drug for its high [[Nicotine|nicotine]] content, and [[Capsaicin|capsaicin]] in Capsicum species gives their fruits pungency.

Electronic device that converts light directly into electricity by the photovoltaic effect. Also called a photovoltaic (PV) cell, it is a type of photoelectric cell and the basic building block of solar panels. Almost all commercial PV cells consist of [[Silicon|crystalline silicon]], with a market share of 95%. Other thin-film technologies include copper indium gallium selenide (CIGS) and amorphous thin-film silicon, while cadmium telluride (CdTe) is the dominant thin-film technology by production volume. A common single-junction silicon cell produces a maximum open-circuit voltage of approximately 0.5 to 0.6 [[Volt|volts]]. Cells also work as photodetectors, such as [[Infrared|infrared]] detectors, and can measure light intensity. Arrays of cells form modules that generate [[Direct current|direct current]], which is often converted to [[Alternating current|alternating current]] by an inverter.

Obscuring of all or part of the [[Sun]] by the [[Moon]], visible from only a small part of [[Earth]]. The Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, and such an alignment occurs approximately every six months, during the eclipse season at new moon. Unlike a [[Lunar eclipse|lunar eclipse]], which can be seen from the whole night side of Earth, a solar eclipse can be viewed only from a relatively small area. Total solar eclipses occur somewhere on Earth about every 18 months on average, but recur at any given place only once every 360 to 410 years. Because the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 [[Degree (angle)|degrees]] to Earth's orbit, there are at least two, and up to five, solar eclipses each year, no more than two of which can be total. In a total eclipse the Sun's disk is fully obscured, whereas partial and annular eclipses obscure only part of it. Looking directly at the Sun can cause permanent eye damage, so only the total phase is safe to view without protection.

Unit of mass in astronomy, equal to approximately 2×10³⁰ kg, the mass of the [[Sun]]. It is used to express the masses of other [[Star|stars]], stellar clusters, nebulae, galaxies and [[Black hole|black holes]]. The solar mass is about 333,000 times the mass of Earth, or 1,047 times the mass of [[Jupiter]]. The Sun's mass cannot be measured directly. It is calculated from the orbital period of a small body, the [[Astronomical unit|astronomical unit]] and the [[Gravitational constant|gravitational constant]], using Kepler's third law. The Sun loses about (2–3)×10⁻¹⁴ solar masses per year through fusion reactions and the [[Solar wind|solar wind]].

Device that converts [[Sunlight|sunlight]] into electricity, made of multiple solar modules of [[Solar cell|photovoltaic (PV) cells]]. The cells produce [[Direct current|direct current]], which an inverter converts to [[Alternating current|alternating current]] where needed. Panels are usually grouped into arrays or systems, mostly in solar farms or on rooftops that supply the electricity grid. They use a renewable, clean energy source and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, but they depend on sunlight, require cleaning and have high initial costs. Russell Ohl's 1939 cell design, patented in 1941, was first used by [[Bell Labs|Bell Labs]] in 1954 to create the first commercially viable silicon solar cell. Since 2010 the cost of solar photovoltaic electricity has fallen 85%.

Conversion of energy from [[Sunlight|sunlight]] into [[Electricity|electricity]], either directly by photovoltaics (PV) or indirectly by concentrated solar power (CSP). PV systems use the photovoltaic effect in [[Solar panel|solar panels]] to convert light into electric current. CSP systems use lenses or mirrors to focus sunlight onto a hot spot, often to drive a [[Steam turbine|steam turbine]]. Commercial CSP plants were first developed in the 1980s. As the cost of solar panels has fallen, grid-connected PV capacity has doubled about every three years, and three-quarters of new generation capacity is solar. Solar generated 7% of global electricity in 2024 and 9% in 2025. Along with onshore [[Wind power|wind power]], utility-scale solar is the cheapest source of new electricity in most countries. [[China|China]] produces 98% of the world's solar wafers, 92% of solar cells and 85% of solar panels.

Stream of charged particles released from the outermost atmospheric layer of the Sun, the corona. It consists mostly of [[Electron|electrons]], [[Proton|protons]] and [[Alpha particle|alpha particles]], with trace amounts of heavy ions and nuclei of elements such as carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, neon, magnesium, silicon, sulfur and iron. The solar wind varies in density, temperature and speed over time and across solar latitude and longitude. Beyond a few solar radii it reaches speeds of 250–750 km/s and is supersonic. The boundary separating the corona from the solar wind is called the Alfvén surface. Related phenomena include the [[Aurora|aurora]], [[Comet|comet]] tails that always point away from the Sun, and geomagnetic storms. In 1859 Richard Carrington and Richard Hodgson made the first observations of a solar flare, and Carrington suspected a connection to a geomagnetic storm the following day.

Process of joining two metal surfaces by heating a filler metal called solder, which melts, flows into the joint and solidifies into a strong, durable bond. Soldering is widely used in the electronics industry to manufacture and repair [[Printed circuit board|printed circuit boards (PCBs)]] and other components. It is also used in [[Plumbing|plumbing]], metalwork and the manufacture of jewelry. Common solders are [[Alloy|alloys]] such as tin-lead, tin-silver and tin-copper, and lead-free solder has become more common because of the health and environmental dangers of lead. Soldering was apparently employed as early as 5,000 years ago in Mesopotamia. Copper, zinc, [[Brass|brass]], silver and gold are easy to solder, while [[Stainless steel|stainless steel]] and some aluminum alloys are more difficult because of their thin, strong oxide films.

Member of an [[Army|army]], either a conscripted or volunteer enlisted person, a non-commissioned officer, a warrant officer or an [[Officer (armed forces)|officer]]. The word derives from Middle English and Old French, meaning mercenary, and ultimately from the Late Latin *solidus*, an ancient Roman coin used in the [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantine Empire]]. Many designations reflect a soldier's specialty, such as trooper, tanker, commando, [[Infantry|infantryman]], artilleryman, paratrooper, medic and sniper. U.S. soldiers are often called G.I.s, a term that came into common use during and after [[World War II|World War II]]. Before and during [[World War I|World War I]], American soldiers were called Doughboys. Women served in Allied forces in World War II, and some were honored as Heroes of the Soviet Union. Race and sex have historically restricted who could serve, and sex-segregated women's branches were disbanded in the last decades of the twentieth century.

Measure of the field of view from a point that a given object covers, expressed in steradians (symbol: sr). The point from which the object is viewed is the apex, and the object is said to subtend its solid angle there. In the International System of Units, a steradian equals one square [[Radian|radian]]. One steradian corresponds to one unit of area on the unit [[Sphere|sphere]] around the apex, so an object blocking all rays from the apex covers 4π steradians. Solid angles can also be measured in square degrees, square arc-minutes and square arc-seconds. A small object nearby can subtend the same solid angle as a larger object farther away: the [[Moon]] and the [[Sun]] appear about the same size from [[Earth]], as seen during a [[Solar eclipse|solar eclipse]]. A solid angle does not measure an object's shape, so a spherical cap and a spherical lune may subtend the same solid angle.

Branch of [[Continuum mechanics|continuum mechanics]] that studies the behavior of solid materials, especially their motion and deformation under the action of [[Force|forces]], temperature changes, phase changes and other agents. It is fundamental to civil, [[Aerospace engineering|aerospace]], nuclear, biomedical and mechanical engineering, to geology, and to branches of physics and chemistry such as [[Materials science|materials science]]. A solid can support a substantial shearing force over a given time scale, which distinguishes it from a fluid. One of the most common practical applications is the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation. Solid mechanics uses [[Tensor|tensors]] to describe stresses, strains and the relationship between them. Its subfields include stability of structures, vibrations, fracture and damage mechanics, and the study of [[Composite material|composite materials]]. Its computational methods include the finite element method.

Computer storage device that uses [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuits]], typically NAND flash memory, to store data persistently. Unlike traditional [[Hard disk drive|hard disk drives]] (HDDs), SSDs have no moving parts, which gives faster data access, lower latency, greater resistance to physical shock, lower power consumption and silent operation. SSDs are used in [[Personal computer|personal computers]], enterprise servers and [[Mobile device|mobile devices]], often interfacing with a system in the same way as HDDs. They are generally more expensive per gigabyte and have a finite number of write cycles. Each memory cell stores one [[Bit|bit]] in single-level cells (SLC), while multi-level, triple-level and quad-level cells (QLC) store more data but offer lower performance and endurance. Solid-state hybrid drives (SSHDs) combine SSD and HDD technologies to improve performance at a lower cost than pure SSDs.

Branch of physics that studies rigid matter, or solids, through methods such as [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]], [[Crystallography|crystallography]], electromagnetism and metallurgy. It is the largest branch of [[Condensed matter physics|condensed matter physics]] and forms the theoretical basis of [[Materials science|materials science]]. Along with solid-state chemistry, it has direct applications in [[Transistor|transistors]] and [[Semiconductor|semiconductors]]. Solids may be held together by ionic bonds, as in sodium chloride, by [[Covalent bond|covalent bonds]], by metallic bonding, or by van der Waals forces, as in the noble gases. Most work focuses on [[Crystal|crystals]], whose periodic atomic arrangement facilitates mathematical modeling. Although solids had been studied for centuries, the field emerged as a separate discipline in the 1940s, when the Division of Solid State Physics was established within the American Physical Society. By the early 1960s it was the society's largest division.

Genus of about 100 to 120 species of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] in the family [[Asteraceae|Asteraceae]], commonly called goldenrod. Most are herbaceous perennials found in open areas such as meadows, prairies and savannas. Most species are native to [[North America|North America]], including Mexico, with a few native to South America and Eurasia. Some American species have been introduced into [[Europe|Europe]] and other parts of the world. Goldenrods bloom in late summer and early fall, and their many species are difficult to tell apart because of their similar golden-yellow flower heads. Propagation is by wind-disseminated [[Seed|seeds]] or by spreading underground rhizomes, which can form colonies of clones of a single plant. Some species produce abundant nectar when moisture is plentiful or the weather is warm and sunny.

Mutual moral and material support among the members of a group in times of need. In the [[Napoleonic Code|Napoleonic Code]], solidarity meant joint liability of debtors toward a common creditor. After the [[French Revolution|French Revolution]], [[Conservatism|conservatives]] detached the concept from the law as a reaction against rapid social change. [[Auguste Comte|Auguste Comte]], the so-called founder of sociology, adopted it to describe social interdependence and linked it to [[Altruism|altruism]]. By the turn of the 20th century the term had become a generic word for progressive values, and the Paris Communards replaced the revolutionary slogan of fraternity with solidarity. [[Émile Durkheim|Émile Durkheim]] distinguished mechanical solidarity, based on the homogeneity of traditional small-scale societies, from organic solidarity, based on the interdependence of specialized work in modern industrial societies, in *The Division of Labour in Society* (1893).

Order of [[Arachnid|arachnids]] known as solifuges, sun spiders, camel spiders or wind scorpions, with more than 1,000 described species in about 147 genera. Despite their common names, they differ from both [[Spider|spiders]] and [[Scorpion|scorpions]]. Most species live in dry climates and feed opportunistically on ground-dwelling [[Arthropod|arthropods]] and other small animals. The largest reach 12–15 cm (5–6 in) including legs, though most are closer to 5 cm (2 in) in body length. Unlike spiders, they lack spinnerets and silk and cannot spin webs. Urban legends exaggerate their size, speed and danger to humans, which is negligible.

Philosophical position that only one's own [[Mind|mind]] is certain to exist. Knowledge of anything outside one's own mind, including the external world and other minds, is uncertain and cannot be conclusively known. Metaphysical solipsism holds that the self is the only existing reality and that other realities are its representations. Epistemological solipsism regards the existence of an external world as an unresolvable question rather than a falsehood. Methodological solipsism is an agnostic variant, often used as a thought experiment to assist [[Skepticism|skepticism]], as in the Cartesian skepticism of [[René Descartes|René Descartes]].

Biblical king of ancient Israel (r. c. 970–931 BC), the son and successor of [[David|David]]. According to the [[Hebrew Bible|Hebrew Bible]], his reign brought commercial prosperity through alliances and trade, but his accumulation of wealth, horses and foreign wives, who introduced [[Idolatry|idolatry]], led to divine punishment. After his death his son Rehoboam's harsh policies led the northern Israelites to reject the Davidic line and split the kingdom into Israel and Judah. Solomon is portrayed as wealthy, wise and a dedicated follower of [[Yahweh|Yahweh]], and is traditionally regarded as the author of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and Song of Songs. In the [[New Testament|New Testament]] he is a teacher of wisdom, and the [[Quran|Quran]] regards him as a major prophet. Current scholarship generally allows for a historical Solomon, but the opulence of his biblical empire is considered highly likely to be an anachronistic exaggeration.

Archipelagic country of six major islands and more than 1,000 smaller ones in [[Melanesia|Melanesia]] and [[Oceania|Oceania]], northeast of [[Australia|Australia]]. It has a total area of 28,896 sq km and a population of 828,857 (pop., 2025). Its capital and largest city, Honiara, is on Guadalcanal. The Spanish navigator Álvaro de Mendaña was the first European to visit the islands, in 1568, and reports of his voyage were conflated with stories of the wealthy biblical [[Solomon|King Solomon]], which gave the islands their name. The southern islands became a British protectorate in June 1893. During [[World War II|World War II]], the [[Guadalcanal campaign|Battle of Guadalcanal]] was a turning point in the Pacific War. The country became independent in 1978 and is a [[Constitutional monarchy|constitutional monarchy]], with [[Charles III|Charles III]] as king.

Archaic Athenian statesman, lawmaker, political philosopher and poet, one of the Seven Sages of Greece. He is credited with laying the foundations of democracy in [[Athens|Athens]]. His reforms included debt relief known as *seisachtheia* ("shaking off of burdens"), and he repealed all of [[Draco (legislator)|Draco's laws]] except those on homicide. According to Diogenes Laërtius he was chosen archon, or chief magistrate, in 594 BC. Around 595 BC, Athenian forces under Solon defeated the Megarians in the dispute over Salamis, and [[Sparta|Spartan]] arbitrators later awarded the island to Athens. [[Aristotle|Aristotle]] called him "the first people's champion", and [[Demosthenes|Demosthenes]] credited his reforms with starting a golden age. Solon's works survive only in fragments, and the main sources, including [[Herodotus|Herodotus]] and [[Plutarch|Plutarch]], wrote long after his death.

Point in the year when the [[Sun|Sun]]'s path reaches its most northerly or southerly extent relative to the celestial equator. Two solstices occur each year, around 20–22 June and 20–22 December, and the term also refers to the day on which this occurs. In many countries the seasons are defined by reference to the solstices and [[Equinox|equinoxes]]. Away from the [[Equator|equator]] and the poles, the summer and winter solstices are the days with the longest and shortest periods of daylight. The word derives from Latin *sol* (sun) and *sistere* (to stand still), because the Sun's motion in declination appears to stop before reversing. When it is the [[Summer solstice|summer solstice]] at one pole, it is the [[Winter solstice|winter solstice]] at the other.

Homogeneous [[Mixture|mixture]] of a solute and a solvent, in which the solvent is the substance present in the greatest amount. The IUPAC defines a solution as a liquid or solid phase containing more than one substance, and calls it dilute when the solutes make up a small share of the mixture. Solvents can be gases, liquids or solids. Air is a gaseous solution, and oxygen dissolved in [[Water|water]] allows fish to breathe underwater. [[Ethanol|Ethanol]] dissolved in water makes alcoholic beverages, and sugar water contains dissolved sucrose. Solid solutions include [[Steel|steel]], essentially carbon atoms in a crystalline matrix of iron atoms, and [[Alloy|alloys]] such as [[Bronze|bronze]]. Hydrogen dissolves well in palladium, a property studied for hydrogen storage. Liquids that can completely dissolve in each other are miscible, and once a solution is saturated, no more solute can dissolve.

Ongoing civil war in [[Somalia|Somalia]] that grew out of resistance to the military junta of Siad Barre in the 1980s. Clan-based armed groups overthrew Barre in 1991, and rival factions then competed for power, leaving Somalia a failed state. UN missions began in 1992, and the UN withdrew in 1995 after an armed conflict between [[Insurgency|insurgents]] and UN troops in 1993. In 2006 Ethiopian troops invaded to depose the Islamic Courts Union and install the Transitional Federal Government. The insurgent Al-Shabaab then fought the Somali government and [[African Union|African Union]] peacekeepers. The Federal Government of Somalia, the country's first permanent central government since the war began, was established in August 2012.

Cushitic language of the Afroasiatic family, spoken primarily in Greater Somalia and by the Somali diaspora. It is an official language in [[Somalia|Somalia]], [[Somaliland|Somaliland]] and [[Ethiopia|Ethiopia]], a national language in [[Djibouti|Djibouti]], and a recognized minority language in [[Kenya|Kenya]]. As of 2021 there were approximately 24 million speakers, about 17 million of them in Somalia. Somali is the best-documented Cushitic language, with academic studies dating back to the late 19th century. Its official script is the [[Latin script|Latin alphabet]], adopted in 1972, although an [[Arabic|Arabic]] alphabet and indigenous scripts such as Osmanya are used informally. Since January 1973 it has been the primary language of administration and education in Somalia. The Regional Somali Language Academy, established in June 2013 in Djibouti City, is mandated to preserve the language.

Country in the [[Horn of Africa|Horn of Africa]], the easternmost country in continental Africa, officially the Federal Republic of Somalia. It borders [[Ethiopia|Ethiopia]] to the west, [[Djibouti|Djibouti]] to the northwest and [[Kenya|Kenya]] to the southwest, with the [[Gulf of Aden|Gulf of Aden]] to the north and the [[Indian Ocean|Indian Ocean]] to the east. It has the longest coastline on the African mainland. Its population is estimated at over 19 million, of whom 2.7 million live in the capital and largest city, [[Mogadishu|Mogadishu]]. About 85% of residents are ethnic Somalis, and the overwhelming majority are Sunni Muslims. The Somali sultanates were colonized by Italian and British empires in the late 19th century and merged into an independent republic in 1960. The country is among the least developed in the world, with an informal economy based mainly on [[Livestock|livestock]], remittances and telecommunications. Insurgents still control much of central and southern Somalia.
